reason: This narrative passage (Genesis 32-33) actually demonstrates the opposite principle. Jacob faces his estranged brother Esau, who approaches with 400 men. Rather than employing violence, Jacob uses strategic non-violent approaches: gift-giving (sending herds ahead), humble submission (bowing seven times), diplomatic language through messengers, and prayerful appeal to God. The reconciliation that follows is entirely peaceful—Esau embraces Jacob with tears and weeping. The text explicitly rejects violence as a leadership model; instead, it portrays humility, generosity, and faithful reliance on God as the means to resolve conflict and earn favor.
